rationale: Pairs a positronic-style brain with organic body structure to gain mobility, which points toward a mobile human-like machine. It says nothing about walking, speech or handling objects, and uses living tissue rather than WABOT-1's mechanics.
Only says robots ('metal people') are descended from human builders on several planets. This implies human-like machines but gives no walking, speaking or manipulation.

Sixteen motor centers coordinated by a central brain loosely evokes a body-wide control system for a movable robot. Nothing is said about a human-shaped body, walking or grasping, and the fluid-electronic mechanism differs.

A domestic robot that is 'physically attractive' and traded for newer models implies a human-looking household servant, matching the humanoid-in-human-surroundings function. The thermostat-speed mechanism is unrelated to WABOT-1 and no walking or grasping is described.

A unit that can powder rock or pick up a pin matches the object-handling capability of a humanoid with hands (WABOT-1 gripped objects). Strength and fine control are asserted without any mechanism, and walking or speech is absent.
A seven-foot android figure acting as a caretaker matches a human-shaped robot operating among people. The quotation shows only its bulk, with no walking, speech or grasping mechanism.
Describes a robot made in man's image and treated as a lower class, so the human-shaped body is present. The passage is about status and gives no walking, talking or manipulation detail.
Mentions purchasable 'pretty automatons' as companions, hinting at human-like machines. The quotation has no capability or mechanism, and the commercial availability is far beyond WABOT-1.
Robots physically carry a person, which shows robots handling people in human settings. Nothing indicates a human shape, bipedal walking or speech.
A 'Mechanical Pugilist' regulated by a fight commission implies a human-form fighting machine. The quotation gives no movement, speech or manipulation mechanism.

A tall humanoid body linked to a person's brain by control channels gives a human-shaped robot that moves and acts in human environments. It is remote-controlled by thought, which WABOT-1 was not, and the quotation lacks walking or speaking detail.
A handsomely built eight-foot robot assembled from parts suggests a human-sized constructed humanoid. The quotation says nothing about how it moves, speaks or grasps.
Praises intelligent, self-controlled robots as a boon to humanity, with no human shape, locomotion or object handling. It only evokes robots generally.
A robot calling itself an extension of its creator's mind is about mind-copying and has no body, walking, speaking or handling content in the quotation.
Mentions being the first of its kind and a failure, a loose echo of a first-prototype humanoid. It contains no description of function or mechanism.
A ship's 'little mechanical' with no say in decisions only implies a robot crewmate. The quotation gives no body shape, locomotion or manipulation.
Androids specialized for particular tasks are only implied, with no description of walking, speaking or handling objects.
A chunky robot body crammed with tool devices hints at a capable machine, but the quotation focuses on its disguised intelligence and says nothing of human form, walking or speech.

A figure with a chest control board that uses servo mechanisms to sit down is a humanoid body with actuated, controlled movement. WABOT-1 shares the human-shaped, servo-driven body, but nothing is said of walking, speech or grasping.
A robot enters a room noisily, so it moves among people, but nothing indicates a human shape or manipulation, and the passage dwells on hissing and clanking.
Speculates that robots will one day become true humanoid copies of their makers. This is an aspiration about form, not a described working machine.
A cybernetic brain in a functional body able to do harm points to an embodied robot, but it states no human shape, walking or speech.
A carpenter robot that strolls off whistling implies a walking, working human-form machine in a human workplace. The brief line gives no mechanism for how it walks or handles tools.

A humanoid upper body with camera eyes and speaker, able to talk and move, matches the talking and perceiving side of WABOT-1. It rolls on tank tracks instead of walking, so the locomotion mechanism differs.
Humanoid-looking machines with jointed limbs that carry out complex tasks match a robot with arms handling things in human-built settings. Limbs are described but walking and speech are not.
A mechanical man with a coin slot in his chest is a human-shaped machine in a joke. No walking, speaking or manipulation function is described.

A mannequin-like robot with a walking control set that conserves its battery matches a walking human-shaped machine. It lacks speech and object handling, and the atomic battery is a different power mechanism.
Max the robot digging in a flower bed shows a robot using tools on objects around a home. The quotation does not state a human shape, walking or speech.
Only says the robot is humanoid in shape and flesh-colored. It describes appearance alone, with no walking, talking or handling.
A boast about building machines that walk and talk (and also fly, swim and bark) loosely evokes the capabilities, but it is generic and not specifically human-shaped.
Says humanoid servants are fashionable among the smart set. This points toward human-form household robots but gives no description of what they do or how.
A figure moves heavy substances and seems to make them obey her command, a loose precursor to commanded machinery doing heavy work. There is no programmable arm or factory setting.

Scores of animate machines working in a large workshop ignore passers-by, which matches autonomous machines doing factory work in place of people. Programmability and a mechanical arm are not described.
Machines given small brains with television sight and hearing evoke sensor-equipped automatons. The quotation does not state the factory, mining or warehouse work.
A robot gardener guiding an electric machine is autonomous labor, but it is garden work and not factory, mining or warehouse work, and there is no programmed arm.
Names a robot wizard's daughter and 'iron monsters' with no labor function, so it is not about work machines in place of laborers.
Commercial robots built for mining on Mars match machines doing mining labor in place of humans. Their programming and arm mechanism are not described.
A tentacled robot seizing people and a swarm of specks in the distance evoke robots at large, but this passage does not show factory or labor tasks.
Robots assisting humans in supplying arms to vessels suggests logistics labor. It gives no detail on machine type, programming or operation.
A company sends a physicist to check its robots, which hints at robots deployed for work. The passage says nothing about their tasks or mechanism.
Robots that need only lubricant and power and tolerate cold and toxic air point to tireless industrial laborers. The quotation gives no task, programming or arm.
Two robot types, one balancing on a gyroscope and a heavy-duty one on tracks, suggest light and heavy duty machines. Their jobs and programmability are not stated.
A corporation turning out thousands of durable robots for industry on two planets matches commercial deployment of industrial robots. How they work or are programmed is not described.
A demountable brain plugged into a larger steam-shovel hints at a reusable controller driving heavy equipment. It does not describe a programmable work machine.
A repair robot whose instructions are changed so it builds finer circuits is a programmable manufacturing machine, as in Unimate. The setting is fictional and no arm is described.

Describes a general-purpose labor robot of limited intelligence next to a single-task repair robot, matching the idea of robots doing human work. Programmability and the mechanical arm are not stated.
A column of eight robots exploring an obstacle like ants shows robots doing road work in a group. It is outdoor clearing, not factory work, and there is no programmable arm.
A metal-faced figure in overalls has taken a farmer's place, which evokes a robot replacing labor. The passage is about impersonation, not a programmed work machine.
Jointed robot stevedores load animals and cages onto a ship, a warehouse and cargo-handling job done in place of people. No programming or controller is described.
States that robots were tried for a wiring task but cannot make decisions and only react. That reaction-only limit loosely resembles a playback-type robot, but no robot work is shown.
Describes giant robots with cylindrical heads and eyes, but only their appearance, with no work function or programmability.
Servo-driven drillers organized into work details on another world match machines doing mining labor under direction. Their programming and manipulators are not described.
Robots scurrying in office tasks that look useless is a general sketch of robots in workplaces, with no factory function or mechanism.
Mindless waldo fingers assembling a unit as officers watch is a manipulator doing assembly work. The passage doesn't say whether it replays recorded motions, which is Unimate's mechanism.
A speaker insists parts are 'powered torsional manipulators', hinting at jointed work limbs. The quotation gives no task, factory setting or programmability.
Blue metal robots with hands, tentacles and grippers show manipulators, but the quotation only describes their build and not any work.
A ten-foot cylinder-bodied robot that 'grated' is a bare mention of a robot with no work function or mechanism.
Boxes on casters with two human-like arms at their sides describe a mechanical arm machine that could do materials-handling work. No task or programming is in the quotation itself.
Robot fitters whose innards suffer in humid conditions imply robots used for assembly work. No mechanism or task detail is given.
A keyed machine whose wire arms turn the pages and pick out words looks up entries mechanically. That is a single code-dictionary lookup, not a store of many records searched on a query.
A central records archive available instantly to offices across a city matches remote access to a large stored collection. The projection display and records scope differ from MEDLINE.

A city-wide library answering calls for records on many subjects from many places matches remote terminals querying a central collection. MEDLINE is text and bibliographic, while this is images and records.
A director speaks a request and gets a printed summary within a moment, matching quick query-driven delivery. It is a computed statistical summary rather than retrieval of stored documents.
A cardex 'chewing on the evidence' to identify a distant ship suggests a card-index machine matching data. The passage gives no query, collection or speed.
A request for all information on a planet points to a search, but librarians work by hand over many days, which is not instant machine search.

A desk cabinet holding over three million items and returning one with its neighbors in about three seconds matches fast machine search of a large collection. It is a card file with no remote terminal or interactive query.
A librarian submits foreign literature to a machine for analysis of idea content. That is content analysis, not finding matching items in a stored collection.

Punching a designation on a keyboard and seeing the record on a screen at once matches interactive terminal lookup. It is retrieval by designation of a single item, not a subject search of literature.
Getting a person's master file through a computer call fits retrieval from a large record store on request. The speaker gives no interface or search mechanism.
A household robot set for a profession class that then finds a person is a database search by attribute. The quotation does not show the results appearing or how long it takes.
A recorded greeting that asks for spoken queries to route a caller is an information-desk front end. It contains no stored collection or matching.
Pressing key combinations on a console while a typer clicks suggests a query entered and results printed. What it searches is unstated.
Robots obtain information from the city library's automatic scanners, so information is fetched from a central store by machine. How the query is made and answered is not described.
A robot whose secondary function is directing technologists to records is a guide to where records are. It does not search them.
A TV reading machine usable with micro-libraries across America suggests remote viewing of stored documents. It is a viewer and not a search service.
A giant machine finds a similar picture in its files, with full details, in seconds, matching fast matching in a large store. It matches by picture and not text queries.
A shipboard collection of audioslides and question-and-answer tapes built to answer any question suggests a media library. Nothing in the passage describes a search.
Loading a history tape into a projector is playback of a chosen recording. No searching or matching occurs.
Asking for every scrap of data on a named subject and getting a fair amount of information matches subject retrieval from a large store. No mechanism for the search is shown.
Coding a query for an unlimited file search through a photoelectric tracer is a machine search of an archive. It matches on a person's description rather than documents on a subject.
A room whose walls hold electronic file controls suggests a large record store. The quotation shows nothing about search.
Says knowledge has grown so vast that machine storage and recall is needed, which is the rationale behind computerized retrieval. It states no search function or speed.
A decision to search the Archives for a man's past and present records is a plan to retrieve records. It does not show how the system works.
Huge punched-card files used because human operatives were too slow match automated storage and lookup of records. Cards are far from online remote terminals.
Putting a photo in a slot and pressing Search is a machine query against a file. It is image matching, not a text search of documents.
Making a quick tape on the cyb to check dates hints at asking a machine for historical records. The passage gives no mechanism or store.
A button press that instantly drops a person's card from a slot is a fast automated record fetch. It is a mechanical card file, not a computer search.
A speaker guesses a ship's model from generator readings, drawing on a directory. The quotation shows only the answer, not retrieval.
A terminal lets users get a recording of any chosen material in print, picture or audio. This fits retrieving stored items on demand from a terminal, though the media differ from MEDLINE's citations.
An information center that can answer any question matches the aim of a very large searchable store. It leaves the mechanism unstated and may rely on human operators.

Dialing the nearest library and asking a robot for information on an institute matches remote querying of a library's holdings from a terminal. The dial-up and robot librarian differ in detail from MEDLINE.
Calls a vertical file a robot memory bank, implying machine storage of records. The passage gives no query or retrieval.
An index in a reading room that readily finds what the reader wants suggests a machine index to a library. How queries are made is not described.
A filing computer that supplies a replacement document within seconds matches machine retrieval of stored documents in seconds. No interactive remote query is shown.
Circuits racing through storage tubes to find a person's record matches a machine searching a large record store. The passage is about the search happening and not the user's query.
Ordering records deleted from tubes and tapes is about erasing a store, not finding items that match a query.
A keyboard and screen set into the wall suggest a terminal for querying a central system. The quotation does not show the query or the results.
Putting a cylinder into an index system to learn everything about a person in two minutes is a machine lookup of a stored record. It is slower than seconds and keyed by the cylinder.
An electronic cross-index added to a library suggests machine indexing of a collection. The quotation gives no query detail.
Submitting an application downstairs for a big computer to work on is a loose hint of a batch lookup. The passage has no retrieval content.
A computer identifies an object by consulting storage banks, a loose match to stored-data lookup. It is classification and not finding records for a query.
A robot answering instantly in a quip is a reply with no retrieval described.
A clerk's button changes an information screen to another list that scrolls briefly. This matches screen-based lookup at a terminal, but the data and search are not described.
A terse reply 'Sirene, 1432. Unsurveyed.' looks like a lookup result, and nothing in the quotation shows a query or collection.
Punching buttons on a machine that returns a packet of cards from a slot is an automated lookup of a person's record. The records are punched cards, not an online search.
Pressing buttons on a reference panel makes screening cards drop from an information bank. This is a machine retrieval by code, not a text query.
A mechanical brain would take time to assemble a list of citizens, so it compiles an answer. It is an offhand statement, not retrieval in seconds.
A brain compares a prospective site with a database and rejects similar ones. This is an automated comparison of candidates rather than retrieving records for a query.
A machine working out a supply list for a ship is calculation and planning, not searching a collection.
Commander extracts yards of stereofac paper from a drawer, implying a record delivered on paper. No search is mentioned.
Dropping a plan to have a machine check colonists' attributes only vaguely implies a record lookup.
Fetching a general map from an information machine is dispensing a prepared item. It involves no query-matching against a large store.
A projected index gives a call number and the text arrives on tape 30 seconds after punching, matching index search and fast delivery from a store. It is a library with no remote terminal.
A machine building that takes in news, indexes it by every category and files it matches building a searchable store. The quotation doesn't show how it is queried.
Machinery that ingests reports from all planets, indexes them by every related category and files them describes building an indexed archive. Retrieval is not shown in this line.
Looking up a planet in a Galactic Directory is a reference lookup. Nothing says it is machine search or fast.
A face is replaced on a screen by a brief on a man, which suggests a record shown on request. The passage doesn't show how it is found.
Feeding in coordinates, and the narrator being preoccupied with them, shows input to a machine. No retrieval is stated.
Feeding entire libraries into a computer's memory and setting it problems stores text and solves problems. It does not find matching items for a query.
Hunting through reference tapes and finding an explicit collection of information on the exact subject matches subject retrieval from stored material. The search method is unstated.
A machinot seated on an electric machine cuts grass with precise movements, so grass cutting is done by a robot. The mower is ridden and guided by the robot, not a self-contained autonomous mower.

A robot-operated lawnmower stops before an obstruction and returns to its path, which matches an autonomous mower detecting and avoiding obstacles. The operator robot is a separate machine in the story, unlike a self-contained MowBot.
An automatic cleaner meant to work alone, here banging around and chasing its owner, matches an autonomous vacuum in function. The quotation offers no mechanism, only comic malfunction.
Robots cleaning automatically while the owner is away match the function of autonomous floor cleaners. The mechanism and form are unspecified, and the robot is not a lawn mower.
Tiny wheeled or floating machines doing many tasks suggests small domestic robots. The quotation never says they clean or mow.

A lawn-tender that leaves its kennel each dry evening to check whether grass needs cutting matches a self-running mower that docks between jobs. The checking-and-watering behavior is richer than MowBot's, and the mechanism is unspecified.
A machine rolling across grass, shifting its own width sideways and returning matches the back-and-forth coverage of an autonomous mower. Its mechanism is only shown by movement.
